posts.title: On forecasting under uncertainty
posts.sub: Models, margins of error, and what "good enough" means in practice.
posts.body:
Every forecast is a confession. It tells you what the forecaster believes, what they're willing to commit to in writing, and — most revealingly — what they're willing to be wrong about. The point is rarely to be *right*. It's to be wrong in a useful direction.

I spent most of 2024 building a forecasting tool called Eddy. The team it served ran a six-hour Friday ritual: pull data from three systems, reconcile, eyeball the residuals, write a one-page memo. The memo was usually correct. It was also, by the time anyone read it, two days late.

## The problem isn't the model

The instinct in this kind of work is to reach for a fancier model. Better features, longer history, a transformer if you're feeling fashionable. But the gap between the team's spreadsheet and the system we replaced it with wasn't accuracy — it was *commitment*. The team gave you a number and a confidence interval. The new system gave you a number and a confidence interval that updated every fifteen minutes whether you were ready or not.

> "Good enough" is a function of who has to act on it, when, and what happens if they're wrong.

That sentence sounds obvious until you try to write it down. Most of the forecasting literature treats the loss function as static — minimise RMSE, optimise log-likelihood, pick your poison. But in production, the loss function is a person. A person who's going to be in a meeting at 9am Monday and needs a number they can defend.

## Three margins worth caring about

Through a year of iteration, three margins kept mattering more than the rest:

`Latency` — how stale is the input by the time the output ships. We collapsed Eddy from a 6-hour batch to a 40-minute pipeline. Not because the math got faster; because we stopped reconciling things that didn't need reconciling.

`Coverage` — the share of the things you're *supposed* to forecast that the system actually has an answer for. A 95% accurate forecast across 60% of the catalogue is worse than a 85% accurate one across 100%.

`Trust decay` — how quickly users stop checking the model when it's quietly wrong. This one's the worst, because by the time you notice, the damage is already done. We started shipping a weekly "look at this graph, here's what surprised us" memo. It wasn't part of the spec. It probably mattered more than the model did.

## What I'd do differently

I'd start with the memo. Build the artefact that the team would publish at the end of the week, then work backwards to the smallest model that could fill it in. Most forecasting projects build the model and then go looking for a reason it matters. That's the wrong direction.

I'd also keep the spreadsheet alive longer. The team's Friday ritual was the source of truth for two years after we shipped. It died eventually, but it died because the new system earned the right to replace it — not because we deprecated the old one out of pride.

If you take one thing from this: the forecast is the small part. The interface to the decision is the work.

posts.title: Three months of training data, one DNF
posts.sub: What the numbers said, what I ignored, and what I would do differently.
posts.body:
Twelve weeks of training. Six different workout types. A DNF at the half-marathon checkpoint of a 70.3.

The garmin file is honest. The story I told myself afterwards was less so.

## What the data said

My resting heart rate climbed three beats per minute over the final two weeks. My HRV dropped into the bottom decile of my baseline. The wattage I held on a tempo bike fell from 230W to 198W for the same perceived effort.

I saw these numbers. I had a spreadsheet. I logged them every morning.

I ignored them anyway, because the plan said taper, and the plan was the plan.

## What I'd change

Write the *stopping rule* before the season starts, not in the moment. If RHR is up three for five days straight, the next session is easy regardless of what the plan says. Decide that in January, not in May at 5am.

The data wasn't the problem. The decision protocol on top of it was.

posts.title: What makes a good brief?
posts.sub: A brief is a design artefact. Most people treat it as a formality.
posts.body:
A bad brief is a fill-in-the-blanks form. A good brief is a piece of writing that, by the end of reading it, gives every participant the same picture of what success looks like.

The difference is whether the brief took anyone *thinking* to write.

## The test

Give the brief to two people who weren't in the room when it was written. Have them sketch what the final deliverable looks like, separately. Compare the sketches. If they don't match, the brief failed — regardless of how complete the fields are.

## What to keep

- The *one* decision the deliverable needs to support
- The audience by name ("the regional managers reading this on a Monday") not role ("stakeholders")
- One example of a previous output that got it right, and one that got it wrong
- The thing you're explicitly *not* doing

That last one matters most. Most briefs grow in scope because no one wrote down what wasn't in scope.

posts.title: Spinout paperwork, for scientists
posts.sub: Notes from building Lab2Launch — what the legal stack actually looks like.
posts.body:
Lab2Launch started as a frustration. Three researchers, three different universities, three completely incompatible spinout processes — and a shared sense that the bottleneck wasn't the science.

The paperwork is not hard in the abstract. It's hard because no one tells you what order it goes in, and the order depends on the institution, the funder, and which solicitor your TTO has on retainer this quarter.

posts.title: Six hours to forty minutes
posts.sub: How a single forecasting workflow at Eddy collapsed an entire weekly ritual.
posts.body:
The six-hour Friday wasn't six hours of work. It was forty minutes of work spread over six hours of context switching.

What we shipped wasn't a faster model. It was a way to *not have to context-switch* — a single page that updated continuously, and a memo template that filled itself in from the latest run.

The maths didn't get faster. The interface to the maths did.
